standard: Standard written American English; sole-answer test includes defensible alternative readings.

choice_assessments.reason: The sum of eight dollars normally takes singular covers, and eight tickets takes plural remain.
The price is one amount; the tickets are separate objects.

choice_assessments.judgment: not natural on the supplied amount reading
choice_assessments.reason: Plural cover would require a strained reading of the dollars as separate objects rather than the price of admission.

items.plural_quantity_agreement_defensible: Only by construing eight separate dollar units as acting individually; the admission-price context does not naturally support that reading.
items.naturalness: Natural enough, though 'Eight tickets remain at the entrance' lacks context for what the tickets are doing there.
items.level_2_3: Yes; straightforward agreement contrast with two blanks.

choice_assessments.reason: Runners is plural, so jogs is wrong, whatever the first-blank reading.
Runners is plural, so jogs is wrong.
Twelve minutes is construed as one period of sufficient length, and runners is plural.
The minutes can be construed as a plural collection that together suffice; 'twelve minutes are enough' is idiomatic for some writers.

within_item_pairs.note: Both agreement choices can convey the same sufficient-duration claim.

items.plural_quantity_agreement_defensible: Yes: 'Twelve minutes are enough for a warm-up' is a viable plural construal; this creates two acceptable answer pairs.
items.naturalness: Both complete sentences are natural; the contrast between minutes and runners is clear.
items.level_2_3: Yes in concept, but the multiple acceptable answers spoil single-choice scoring.

choice_assessments.reason: Hikers is plural; three miles is one remaining distance.
A writer may construe the remaining miles as plural stretches, even though the route-distance reading favors is.
Three hikers requires rest, regardless of the distance reading.

within_item_pairs.note: The quantity versus plural-stretches construal is subtle and does not change the practical claim.

items.plural_quantity_agreement_defensible: Yes, though less strongly than in M2: 'Three miles are all that remains' can treat the remaining miles as multiple stretches. Singular is clearly preferable for one remaining distance.
items.naturalness: The hiking context is natural. 'Three miles is all that remains to the next campsite' is slightly stiff; 'Three miles remain before the next campsite' would read more smoothly, but it would alter the test.
items.level_2_3: Yes in concept; the plural-distance alternative weakens a single-answer item.

choice_assessments.reason: The limit is one five-pound weight, and parcels requires need.

choice_assessments.judgment: not natural on the supplied limit reading
choice_assessments.reason: A single stated weight limit strongly calls for is; plural are would need a contrived reference to individual pounds.
Five pounds names one weight threshold, whereas five parcels are counted objects.

items.plural_quantity_agreement_defensible: No plausible plural reading in the given sentence: the phrase denotes one weight limit for each parcel.
items.naturalness: Natural, although 'Five parcels need labels before shipping' is generic and context-light.
items.level_2_3: Yes; straightforward agreement contrast with two blanks.

set_assessment.new_mechanism: The quantity-as-one-unit versus counted-objects contrast is a genuine agreement mechanism distinct from proximity, inversion, and relative-clause agreement. It hinges on construal of a quantified noun phrase rather than identifying a displaced or embedded controller.
set_assessment.repetitiveness: High. All four items repeat a quantified measure plus an equal-number plural count noun in two short independent sentences, with a two-by-two grid of singular/plural verb forms. Reversing sentence order in M3 does little to vary the reasoning. M2 and M4 are especially close; M1 and M4 share the same amount-first/count-first structure, as do M2 and M4.

strong_near_duplicate_cross_item_pairs.reason: Same amount-first/count-second pattern, singular copula for a threshold or sufficiency judgment, then a plural count subject with a present-tense verb.
Both contrast a singularly construed amount with the same-number counted objects in adjacent sentences and test the same two agreement switches.
Same order and same repeated numeral pattern; lexical context alone changes.
Time and distance quantities are paired with people, with the two sentence types simply reversed.
Distance or weight as a singular quantity is paired with a counted plural noun; only order and setting vary.
Same mechanism and two-by-two distractor grid, with the order of amount and counted subject reversed.

set_assessment.overall: The set is suitable only as rough practice. It is too repetitive for four distinct assessment slots, and M2 and M3 lack a safely unique answer under a defensible plural-quantity reading.
set_assessment.recommendation: Keep at most one of these items, preferably M4 or M1, and replace the others with genuinely different grammatical mechanisms or contexts that unambiguously force the intended reading.

reference.title: MLA Style Center, What Is the Difference between Fewer and Less?
